idiom_name: threading.Lock/RLock held as an attribute and acquired with `with`
implementation_notes: Python locks are separate objects rather than per-object monitors - the documentation notes that where Java makes locks and condition variables basic behaviour of every object, they are separate objects in Python - so the class owns a threading.Lock (or RLock for reentrancy) and either publishes it (attribute or lock() accessor) or wraps its methods in `with self._lock:`. A primitive Lock is not owned by a thread when locked (any thread may release it), an RLock records owning thread and recursion level, and both support the context-management protocol, which the docs recommend over manual acquire()/release() because it releases on every exit path. The GIL is not a substitute for the lock: it does not make read-modify-write sequences atomic, and free-threaded builds make the distinction explicit.
pitfalls: threading.Lock is not reentrant: a method that acquires the published lock and then calls another method of the same object that also acquires it deadlocks - use RLock or keep unlocked internal helpers.
Any thread may release a non-reentrant Lock (there is no owner tracking), so a stray release silently removes protection; acquire only through `with` and let the context manager pair the calls.
Blocking acquisition ignores timeouts unless they are requested: acquire(blocking=False) and acquire(timeout=...) exist and should be used wherever liveness matters.
The GIL hides races only for single bytecodes; compound operations still interleave, and on free-threaded (no-GIL) builds (PEP 703) every shared-state assumption must rest on real locks.
